title: Reporting of Positive Results in Randomized Controlled Trials of Mindfulness-Based Mental Health Interventions

selection.evidence: Chosen 2026-11-05 as the clinical/meditation face of excess significance (same session as maglio2014 TIVA and pawel2020). Prior belief: the excess is real; prior suspicion of the paper's method: its expected-positives count rests on one assumed effect size (d = .55), which I want to vary.

cost.compute_notes: PLoS PDF (18 pp, read 1-14) + 7 supplements (docx/doc); S3 Appendix table parsed from document.xml (124 trials: n per arm, power, positivity). Python: Table 1 and d = 1.03 reproduced; equicorrelated-outcome Monte Carlo over k in {1,2,3,4,6}, rho in {.3,.5,.7}, d in {0,.2,.3,.44,.55}, 4,000 reps per trial per cell. c02: PubMed E-utilities search per trial (124 queries; 75 unique matches). c03: 75 abstracts read and coded by hand against PLAN_c03_code_k.md (committed c33365b before reading).

claims.statement: 108 of 124 mindfulness-based therapy RCTs (87%) report at least one positive mental-health outcome in the abstract, 1.6 times the 65.7 expected if every trial had d = 0.55 power; the observed count would require d = 1.03. The excess is concentrated in low-power trials (power < .25: 10 observed vs 2.8 expected; >= .75: 26 vs 26.1).
claims.scope: RCTs vs inactive controls, searched July 2013; 'positive' = >= 1 significant between-groups outcome in the abstract, or within-group if none (Kyzas method); power from the per-arm n in S3 Appendix.

quantities.name: mbt_expected_positive_trials_d055
quantities.baseline: observed 108; reproduced exactly (max |power diff| vs S3 0.0005)

quantities.name: mbt_d_needed_for_observed_positives
quantities.baseline: paper 1.03; 0.807 if only the 94 between-groups positives are counted

our_assessment.why: Every number reproduces. But the numerator and the denominator use different definitions of 'positive': the observed count is 'at least one of several outcomes significant (14 of 108 by a within-group test)', the expected count is single-test between-groups power. With k equicorrelated outcomes and NO reporting bias, the expected count at d = .55 rises to 91.4 (k = 3 for every trial, rho = .5). CORRECTED 2026-11-05 the same day, after coding k from 75 abstracts (c4): with each trial's own k (median 3, many trials at 1-2) honest multiplicity closes about 44% of the gap at d = .55, not 'most' -- a constant k overstates P(any) because it is concave in k. Do not quote the constant-k sweep as the correction. The paper notes it could not identify a primary outcome; it does not carry that into the expected count.

claims.statement: Excess positives survive the multiplicity correction at plausible effect sizes: at d = .44 (top of the AHRQ meditation range .22-.44 the paper cites) honest multiplicity gives 76.5-89.9 expected (k = 3-6, rho = .5) vs 108 observed (ratio 1.20-1.41); at d = .30 it gives 51.5-66.6 (ratio 1.6-2.1). Counting only the 94 between-groups positives against 110 trials, d = .44 and k = 4 give about 73 expected (ratio ~1.29).
claims.scope: k (mental-health outcomes per abstract) is not in the appendices; swept 1-6. Equicorrelated z-approximation; no heterogeneity. The 110-trial figure scales the 124-trial expectation by 110/124 because the 14 within-group-only trials are not identified.

our_assessment.why: The direction of the paper's conclusion stands at any d <= .44 and k <= 6; its magnitude (1.6x, 'd = 1.03 needed') is a property of single-test accounting and should not be quoted as the size of the reporting bias. The honest excess is ~1.2-2x and depends on two numbers nobody measured (k and the true d). SUPERSEDED as an estimate by c4 (coded k): the sweep's constant-k cells overstate the correction; c4 is the number to use.

claims.statement: Of 21 MBT trial registrations completed by 2010, 13 (62%) were unpublished 30 months after completion; none adequately specified a single primary outcome (2/21 adequate if metric not required); 0 of 36 systematic reviews concluded that reporting biases inflated effects.
claims.scope: Registries searched for trials completed by 31 Dec 2010; reviews published 2011-2013.

quantities.name: mbt_registered_unpublished_30mo
quantities.baseline: NIH-funded trials (Ross et al.): 54% unpublished at 30 months -- the paper itself calls MBT 'slightly lower' publication

our_assessment.why: Transcribed, not recomputed (S4 not parsed). 8/21 published vs the NIH 46% is well within binomial noise (n = 21); the registry evidence speaks to poor outcome pre-specification more than to differential non-publication.

claims.statement: Coding k (mental-health outcomes with a between-groups result in the abstract) for the 75 trials matched in PubMed (pre-registered plan, one coder): median 3, mean 3.18; 73.7% of reported outcomes are significant and 39 of 68 trials report ALL their abstract outcomes as significant. In this subsample 69 are positive; single-test expectation at d = .55 is 45.6; honest multiplicity with each trial's own k gives 55.8 at d = .55 and 46.8 at d = .44 (rho .5). By the rule written before coding, the excess survives at d = .44 (shortfall 32% of observed); tripling every k still leaves 58.7 vs 69.
claims.scope: 75 of 124 trials (PubMed first-author/year/journal match; dissertations and non-indexed journals excluded); abstract k is a LOWER bound on outcomes tested; 8 coded unclear (k set to 1).

quantities.name: mbt_reported_outcomes_significant_share
quantities.baseline: 39 of 68 trials report only significant outcomes in the abstract

our_assessment.why: This turns the sweep into an estimate and it lands on the paper's side: multiplicity explains part of the excess (about 10 of 23 extra positives at d = .55), not most of it. The remaining excess is consistent with selective reporting in the abstract itself (three quarters of the outcomes an abstract names are significant), which the paper's own definition of 'positive' already rewards. One coder, convenience subsample: a second coder on a 20-trial overlap would settle the coding.

datasheet.caveats: The number of mental-health outcomes per abstract (k) -- the quantity that decides the expected count under the paper's positivity rule -- is not recorded anywhere in the supplements.

relations.why: Same excess-significance logic (observed vs power-expected significant results); there per paper, here per literature.

Both compare an observed count with a model-expected count; in both the expected count's definition carries assumptions (single test here, forecast family there) that move the gap more than the literature does.
